item.title: JAXA's Martian Moons eXploration Mission is on its Way to Mars and Phobos
item.description: JAXA successfully launched its Martian Moon eXplorer on its way to Mars and Phobos. It'll reach Mars in about six months, and will orbit the planet for about a month before transferring to an orbit around Phobos. It will deploy a small lander, which will help select a sample-gathering location for the main part of the mission. By 2031, the regolith sample from Phobos should be back on Earth.

item.title: Japan to launch world-first mission to moon of Mars
item.description: Japanese scientists will launch a spacecraft on Tuesday that aims to be the first to retrieve samples from one of Mars' moons, potentially helping unlock the origins of the solar system and life on Earth.

item.title: Mars moon lander set to launch on 19 October
item.description: The Martian Moons eXploration ( MMX ) mission is set to launch into space on a H3 rocket from the Tanegashima Space Center at 04:41 JST on 20 October 2026 (20:41 BST / 21:41 CEST on 19 October 2026). MMX will be the first mission to collect a sample from Mars’s moon Phobos and bring it back to Earth. item.title: Japan launches spacecraft to mysterious moons of Mars in a bold mission to bring home soil samples
item.description: A Japanese spacecraft rocketed toward Mars on Tuesday on a quest to explore its mysterious moons and bring back samples.

item.title: Scientists Use Ancient Rains to Map the Possible Origin Life on Mars
item.description: Billions of years ago, rain may have helped shape where the chemistry of life could begin on Mars. A new study maps how formaldehyde, an important prebiotic molecule, may have reached the surface. This map could help guide future missions searching for signs of past life on Mars.

item.title: 2026 Full Moon calendar: When to see the Full Moon and phases
item.description: The phenomenon of a Full Moon arises when our planet, Earth, is precisely sandwiched between the Sun and the Moon. This alignment ensures the entire side of the Moon that faces us gleams under sunlight. item.title: Mars’s Most Mysterious Cloud Might Be Defying Textbook Cloud Physics
item.description: It may not be as obvious, but just like Earth, Mars has seasons. And every day of every summer, an 1,800 kilometer long thin white cloud appears to the west of Arsia Mons, a 20 kilometer high extinct shield volcano. At least for a few hours, before it dissipates until it reappears the next morning. item.title: The Moon is Still Shrinking as it Cools. That Could Create a Hazard for Lunar Mission.
item.description: The Moon is slowly cooling and slowly shrinking. A study of its scarp faults calculates the rate of shrinkage, showing that it's extremely small. But the shrinking could still create landslides, a potential hazard for missions to the lunar surface.

item.title: The ESA's Euclid Space Telescope Has Discovered A New Comet
item.description: The ESA's Euclid space telescope was launched in July, 2026, and its mission is to observe billions of galaxies. The goal is to measure their redshifts over 10 billion years of Universal expansion, to better understand dark matter and dark energy. Surprisingly, the telescope has discovered a brand new comet, now named C/2026 S1 (Euclid).

item.title: Euclid discovers new comet
item.description: The European Space Agency’s Euclid space telescope has discovered its first previously unknown comet, in images taken between 16 and 24 September 2026.

item.title: Japan is launching a mission to Mars’s largest moon Phobos
item.description: The Martian Moons eXploration spacecraft, set to launch on 20 October, will bring back samples that should solve a moon mystery that has been vexing scientists for more than a century

item.title: Mars’s oddest cloud may be even odder than we thought
item.description: Scientists using the European Space Agency's Mars Express , in combination with a state-of-the-art meteorological model of the Red Planet, have found that there may be some very exotic physics behind Mars’s most curious cloud.

item.title: 'Terror of kings': Why the 1066 appearance of Halley's Comet terrified the medieval world
item.description: A sequence on the Bayeux Tapestry shows King Harold alongside a crowd gazing at the sky, beneath the embroidered caption Isti mirant stella ("those people marvel at the star"). Above Harold sits Halley's Comet, with ghostlike invasion boats in the border below—a Norman framing of Harold as a doomed usurper whose betrayal invited destruction.

item.title: NASA experimental Mars helicopter blade designs target longer flights
item.description: NASA researchers are developing the future of flight on Mars, laying the groundwork for helicopters with the ability to fly higher and farther while conducting science on the Red Planet. Using high-fidelity computer simulations and wind tunnel tests, engineers are reimagining the rotorcraft blades that could carry the next generation of Mars flyers.

item.title: Hot plasma may explain how rapidly feeding black holes launch powerful jets
item.description: Some supermassive black holes rapidly consume surrounding matter while simultaneously firing powerful streams of plasma into space at nearly the speed of light. However, this creates a physical puzzle: rapid feeding is expected to form a cold, flat accretion disk around the black hole, which prevents powerful jets from forming.

item.title: Giant canyon on Mars is still tectonically active today
item.description: Scientists at Columbia University and Imperial College London have found that the largest canyon system in the solar system is still active and shaping Mars today, billions of years after it first formed.

item.title: Who speaks for Mars? Scientists call for ethical debate before terraforming begins
item.description: Transforming Mars into a more Earth-like world could irreversibly destroy scientific evidence about the planet's history and the possibility of extraterrestrial life. In an opinion article published in Eos, a team of Dutch, French and U.S. planetary scientists and ethicists warns that humanity risks destroying Mars' scientific record before it has been fully explored.

item.title: Study: Rocks from Mars’ Jezero Crater, which likely predate life on Earth, contain signs of water
item.description: The presence of organic matter is inconclusive, but the rocks could be scientists’ best chance at finding remnants of ancient Martian life.

item.title: Study determines the original orientations of rocks drilled on Mars
item.description: The “oriented” samples, the first of their kind from any planet, could shed light on Mars’ ancient magnetic field.

item.title: High-orbit satellites could light the way for travel to the moon
item.description: Acting as cooperative optical beacons, the satellites could provide GPS-like navigation and communications support for spacecraft operating across cislunar space.

item.title: Scientists pin down the origins of the moon’s tenuous atmosphere
item.description: The barely-there lunar atmosphere is likely the product of meteorite impacts over billions of years, a new study finds.

item.title: Fly around Schiaparelli Crater with Mars Express
item.description: Video: 00:04:10 ESA’s Mars Express takes us on another mesmerising flight, this time around one of the biggest craters on Mars. Despite measuring a huge 460 km across, Schiaparelli Crater seems to be relatively shallow. Perhaps it has been filled in over the last few billion years by sediment blown by the wind or deposited by water, by lava – or by a combination of all three. item.title: Fueling a return journey from Mars
item.description: PhD candidate Lanie McKinney is building technology to convert the Red Planet’s atmosphere into propellant for bringing astronauts home.

item.title: Lincoln Laboratory laser communications terminal launches on historic Artemis II moon mission
item.description: High-definition video and data sent from the lunar vicinity to Earth will demonstrate the first use of laser communications on a crewed mission.

item.title: Polar weather on Jupiter and Saturn hints at the planets’ interior details
item.description: New research may explain the striking differences between the two planets’ polar vortex patterns.

item.title: MIT engineers prepare to send three payloads to the moon
item.description: Data from the devices will help future astronauts navigate the moon’s south polar region and search for frozen water.

item.title: Life on Mars, together
item.description: With Project MADMEN, two MIT students experience the challenges and bonding associated with a Mars analog mission.
